clinicalPearls: Injury combines a penetrating or laceration wound from the barbed spine with envenomation by a heat-labile venom
Pain is typically immediate, intense and out of proportion to the visible wound
Immersion of the affected part in hot (not scalding) water helps relieve pain by denaturing the venom
Retained spine or sheath fragments in the wound are common and can be missed
Wounds are prone to secondary infection, including marine organisms, so wound care and consideration of antibiotics are important
Truncal or penetrating chest and abdominal wounds can be life-threatening and need urgent surgical assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Stingray injury results from the tail spine penetrating tissue while releasing venom from glandular tissue along the spine. The venom is a heat-labile mixture that causes intense local pain, vasoconstriction and tissue injury, while the barbed spine produces mechanical laceration and can retain fragments. Local necrosis and a high infection risk follow from the combination of envenomation, tissue trauma and contamination, and deep penetrating wounds may damage vital structures.
additionalInvestigations: Wound exploration and imaging to identify retained spine fragments
Assessment of the depth and structures involved, especially for truncal wounds
Consideration of tetanus status and infection risk
Observation for systemic symptoms in severe envenoming
Surgical review for deep or penetrating body-cavity wounds
redFlags: Penetrating chest, abdominal or neck wounds
Signs of systemic envenoming or haemodynamic compromise
Evidence of deep infection or necrosis
reference.prognosis: Most limb injuries do well with hot-water analgesia, wound care and removal of foreign material, but truncal penetrating wounds and severe infections can be serious or fatal.
pitfalls: Failing to search for and remove retained spine fragments
Prematurely closing a contaminated marine wound
Underestimating pain and delaying hot-water immersion
Missing deep penetrating injury to vital structures
management: Immediate hot-water immersion at a tolerable, non-scalding temperature to denature the heat-labile venom and relieve pain
Wound exploration, irrigation and removal of retained spine or sheath fragments, leaving wounds open to heal by secondary intention
Analgesia, including local anaesthetic infiltration or regional block for severe pain
Tetanus prophylaxis and thorough wound cleaning
Antibiotics covering marine organisms such as ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for Vibrio in high-risk or infected wounds
Urgent surgical assessment for truncal or body-cavity penetrating wounds that may injure vital structures
Observe for secondary infection and systemic features of severe envenoming
